Thanks Irene — technical note from Product/Runtime:

Current behavior (short):
- Hosted API: we keep request/response logs and KV cache metadata for up to 30 days by default to support rate-limiting, billing, and debugging. We treat model-generated outputs as ephemeral and do not persist them beyond transactional logs unless a customer opts into logging.
- Dedicated/Private: by default, we do not upload inference outputs to our control plane for Private deployments. Dedicated customers on our managed plane can choose retention settings; Private (VPC/air-gapped) deployments are under customer control and Redwood does not retain outputs unless explicitly configured.

Options we can offer to Pulse:
1) No-retention profile: system will not persist inference outputs beyond in-memory cache (no logs). This disables some debugging features and makes reproducing rare failures harder.
2) 7-day retention: middle ground — minimal window for transient debugging and QoS.
3) 30-day retention (default).

Operational tradeoffs:
- No-retention requires additional instrumentation (client-side request ids) for debugging; support load increases for rare repros.
- Shorter windows may block telemetry-based quality monitoring unless aggregated telemetry is used (see Laura).

Subprocessor visibility: We maintain a Subprocessors page listing all vendors and which components they access. For Hosted we can commit to providing a whitelist and 30-day notice for any new subprocessors with an option for Pulse to opt-out of using a new subprocessor for Dedicated. For Private, customers manage their own subprocessor list.

Suggested redline language (draft):
"Redwood will not retain raw inference outputs derived from Customer Data for more than 7 days by default for the Customer’s account, except where Customer has explicitly enabled longer retention for debugging or product features. For Dedicated or Private deployments, retention is subject to the configuration agreed in writing by the Parties. Access to stored inference outputs will be limited to personnel with documented business need and will be subject to access logging and KMS encryption."

I can tighten wording with Legal.

— Dev
Product Manager, Runtime

Thanks Dev — security take and proposed mitigations to include in contract language:

Risk summary:
- Inference outputs can contain PHI or sensitive derivative data; retention increases risk surface for unauthorized access or inadvertent leakage.
- Subprocessors that operate caching, telemetry, or vector DBs may have potential access to outputs depending on architecture.

Compensating controls we can commit to:
- Default retention settable by Customer (No-retention / 7d / 30d) with clear admin toggle and audit records.
- KMS-wrapped encryption for persisted outputs with separate key management options for Dedicated (Redwood-managed KMS) and Private (customer-provided KMS).
- Strict RBAC for access to persisted outputs; require a documented approval workflow for debug access that includes justification, TTL for access, and automated audit trail export.
- Subprocessor transparency: provide an exported manifest (csv) of current subprocessors and commit to 30-day advance notice for additions. For subprocessors with potential access to stored outputs, we will procure written contractual assurances (SOC2 or equivalent) and optionally place them on a restricted allowlist for Pulse.

Recommended contract clause (short):
"Customer shall have the ability to configure inference-output retention for its account to one of the following profiles: No-retention, 7 days, or 30 days. Any persisted inference outputs will be encrypted at rest with keys managed per the deployment configuration and access to persisted outputs will be restricted to authorized personnel under documented approval and auditing procedures. Redwood will provide Customer with a current manifest of subprocessors and 30 days’ notice prior to engaging any new subprocessor; for subprocessors with access to persisted outputs, Redwood shall obtain written security assurances and provide Customer the option to block such engagement for the duration of negotiation."

If Legal wants slightly looser language (e.g., replace enumerated retention values with "reasonable timeframe") I recommend keeping enumerated options — procurement teams like specifics.

— Laura
Director, Product Security

Hi Tim — thanks for the clear ask and for the redline. We've reviewed internally (Product and Security input included) and attached a proposed tracked-changes document (redline_suggested_language.docx) that reflects a compromise we expect is acceptable for Pulse:

- Enumerated retention options (No-retention / 7-day / 30-day) with default at 7 days for Hosted.
- Explicit customer toggle and documented debug exception process (requires documented justification, automatic TTL, and audit export).
- Subprocessor manifest disclosure and 30-day notice; for subprocessors with access to persisted outputs Redwood will provide written security assurances and an allowlist option for Pulse on Dedicated.

We can represent the final agreement as an addendum to the DPA or an appendix — whichever is easiest for your contracts team. To speed acceptance we’ve generated a DocuSign packet (Pulse_DocSign_Request.url) with the addendum attached; if you prefer tracked changes in your format we can shift.

If Pulse is comfortable, please sign the DocuSign packet. If you'd like wording changes, we can iterate quickly — happy to jump on a 20m call.

Best regards,
